item.title: Postal codes and tessellations
item.description: From postal points to areas using Voronoi polygons
item.content:encoded:
From postal points to areas using Voronoi polygons

<p>I recently published my project <a href="https://dieghernan.github.io/codigospostales/">Postal codes of Spain</a>, with estimated postal areas, an interactive map and GeoPackage downloads. But there is something we have not looked at yet: how do those address points become polygons? The answer is… <strong>Voronoi polygons</strong>. </p>

item.dc:creator: Diego HH
item.title: Let’s peel the world
item.description: Do you know the interrupted Goode homolosine projection?
item.content:encoded:
Do you know the interrupted Goode homolosine projection?

<p>What would happen if we peeled the Earth like an orange? The <a href="https://proj.org/en/stable/operations/projections/igh.html">interrupted Goode homolosine projection</a> gives us something close to that! This equal-area projection preserves relative areas while splitting the world map into lobes. Add a few shades of orange and our world is ready to peel. </p>
item.media:title: Let’s peel the world

A development diary: context, small screens and useful answers

<p>This website uses my <strong>Jekyll</strong> theme, <a href="https://dieghernan.github.io/chulapa"><span class="chulapa">Chulapa</span></a>. item.description: The rain in Spain does not stay mainly in the plain
item.content:encoded:
The rain in Spain does not stay mainly in the plain

<p class="alert alert-info p-3 mx-2 mb-3"><strong>Updated on October 25, 2026:</strong> The elevation and precipitation maps now use <strong>ggblend</strong> to multiply their colors with the hillshade, following <a href="https://barney.fly.dev/2026/01/27/ggplot2-blending-adventure/">Barney Harris’s blending adventure</a>. The map and marginal profiles now share the same precipitation palette and limits. Dominic Royé also demonstrates how to use <strong>ggblend</strong> in <a href="https://dominicroye.github.io/blog/hillshade-effect/">Hillshade effects</a>. </p>

item.title: Head/tail breaks in the classInt package
item.content:encoded: <blockquote class="blockquote"> <p class="small font-italic">There are far more ordinary people (say, 80 percent) than extraordinary people (say, 20 percent), and this is often characterized by the 80/20 principle, based on the observation made by the Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto in 1906 that 80% of land in Italy was owned by 20% of the population. A histogram of the data values for these phenomena would reveal a right-skewed or heavy-tailed distribution. How to map the data with the heavy-tailed distribution? </p></blockquote>

item.title: Quick R: Inset maps
item.description: An alternative using plot()
item.content:encoded:
An alternative using plot()

<p>How to place an inset map in <strong>R</strong>? There are many solutions out there using the <strong>ggplot2</strong> package (see <a href="https://www.r-spatial.org/r/2018/10/25/ggplot2-sf-3.html">Drawing beautiful maps programmatically with <strong>R</strong>, <strong>sf</strong> and <strong>ggplot2</strong></a> by Mel Moreno and Mathieu Basille). However, I like the old reliable <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">plot</code> function, so the question is: is there another way? </p>
item.media:title: Quick R: Inset maps

<p>This is a quick post on how to create a map according to the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Maps/Conventions#Gradient_maps">Wikipedia conventions</a>. In this case, I have chosen to plot the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organ_donor_rates">international organ donor rates</a>, retrieved on February 10, 2019, although the data refers to 2017 (source: <a href="http://www.irodat.org/?p=database">IRODaT</a>). </p>
item.media:title: Wikipedia maps (I): Organ donor rates

item.dc:creator: Diego HH
item.title: Beautiful maps with R (I): Fishnets, honeycombs and pixels
item.description: Simplified maps with R
item.content:encoded:
Simplified maps with R

<p>Sometimes you want to produce maps with special layouts. I especially like maps with modified geometries, e.g. simplifying the original shapes to squares or dots. When searching the web, I found the fantastic post <a href="https://strimas.com/post/hexagonal-grids/">Fishnets and Honeycomb: Square vs. Hexagonal Spatial Grids</a> by <a href="https://strimas.com/#about">Matt Strimas-Mackey</a>, which was a huge inspiration (by the way, don’t miss <a href="http://strimas.com/#posts">his blog</a>, full of very interesting pieces of work). </p>
item.media:title: Beautiful maps with R (I): Fishnets, honeycombs and pixels
